units.text: We'll follow a queued Batch job and decide where it can run. Match the compute environment to the job's resources and runtime, then check the queue points to that environment. For example, a job that requires specialized E C two hardware won't fit a generic Fargate configuration.

Even when Batch can place the job, the container must be able to pull its image and reach inputs and outputs. Check the subnet paths, endpoint or internet access as appropriate, and execution or task permissions. Capacity does not fix a missing data path.

If queued work keeps rising, check which jobs can actually be placed. Compare the requested resources, available capacity and configured limits. A runnable job can be waiting for a compatible slot even though a compute environment exists.

Adding capacity helps when there's a capacity shortage. It won't fix a job asking for resources unavailable in that environment. Find the reason in job status, and test whether the same job moves through the queue after the change.

Some jobs divide one calculation across communicating nodes rather than running independent copies. Batch must place the requested set, then the main and worker nodes cooperate. If it can't assemble that capacity, the job can't start.

Use a supported E C two compute environment for multi-node parallel jobs, not Fargate or Spot. Confirm compatible instance capacity and networking across the nodes before blaming the application for a job that cannot be scheduled.

We'll choose an E M R engine by the kind of processing it needs to do. Spark can run distributed transformations, while other supported engines may better fit interactive S Q L or a specialized workload. Start with the workload, not the cluster shape.

An engine is the tool executing the work; deployment controls how that tool runs and how much infrastructure you manage. Match the runtime and integrations too, so an engine that fits on paper still has access to its data and libraries.

Follow the data into the job. Durable S three storage gives the input and results a home that can outlive the cluster. Cluster-local or distributed working storage can help computation, but don't leave the only copy of important results there.

When an engine reads shared objects or catalog metadata, it needs both the route and intended permissions. Verify the job can read the named inputs and write its result to the durable location before removing the cluster.

The primary node coordinates. Core nodes process data and provide distributed storage for a cluster using H D F S. Task nodes supply additional processing without holding H D F S data. The distinction matters when you add or lose capacity.

For elastic compute, adding task nodes can improve throughput without adding H D F S capacity. If the constraint is distributed storage, adding task nodes doesn't solve it. Select and scale the role the workload actually needs.

An instance group contains instances of one specified type. A fleet can use eligible alternatives to meet a capacity target. That's useful when satisfying the target matters more than obtaining one exact type.

Decide which roles need predictable capacity and which can accept more flexibility or interruptions. Then verify the actual resources acquired, rather than treating the configured target as proof the cluster is already ready.

We'll choose a service for a job by following its work. A short event handler fits Lambda if it meets the invocation limits. A packaged job needing scheduled, configurable compute fits Batch. A distributed analytics job may need an engine such as E M R or Glue.

If the requirement is to coordinate several actions, use a workflow to own the sequence. The workflow can call the appropriate runtime; it doesn't silently replace the compute engine that must transform the data.

Follow the input into a Glue job. The job reads the source, applies the transformations, and writes the intended output. That processing changes data; it is not the same operation as discovering the schema of the files.

Check the job run and inspect the resulting objects or table, not just the completion status. For incremental processing, check how the job tracks prior inputs and how a retry avoids writing duplicate results.

A crawler can inspect configured sources and infer schema and partitions. It writes that metadata to the Data Catalog; it doesn't transform the underlying files. That distinction tells you whether to rerun discovery or run an E T L job.

If a new partition isn't visible in a query, compare the catalog entry with the actual object layout. Verify the query principal has permission to read the metadata and data, then test a query that selects that partition.

We'll follow a warehouse query. The client connects to the endpoint, and the warehouse coordinates execution across compute. The result depends on how data is stored and how much work each compute slice performs, not just whether the S Q L is accepted.

Fit the architecture to the workload's data size and query profile. The compute and storage behavior depends on the deployment type. Verify typical query execution and capacity before assuming you need a bigger warehouse.

A bulk load can use COPY to read approved input from S three rather than inserting every row separately. Give the warehouse the required access to the input; being able to connect to the database doesn't give it permission to read the object.

Check where clients connect, the network controls, transport encryption and database permissions. A client that reaches the endpoint still needs authorization to query data. Confirm the load and query separately to see which gate failed.

Pick the snapshot that meets the recovery objective, restore it to the supported destination, and verify the data. A successful snapshot operation is evidence a recovery point exists, not that the application is already restored.

Test queries and client access after restoration. The recovery time ends when the workload reaches the agreed usable state. The data-loss target depends on the selected recovery point, not merely on having snapshots enabled.

For copying a provisioned K M S-encrypted warehouse snapshot with a customer managed key, configure the destination encryption permission and snapshot copy grant. The source key does not authorize use of the destination key. Serverless uses its own copy configuration and grant handling, so check the deployment type first.
Verify that the copy appears and can be restored in the destination Region. Then test the data and access. Snapshot copy creates a recovery option; it does not make the target a live replica.

We'll query lake files without loading all of them into warehouse tables. Spectrum uses external table metadata to locate and interpret S three data. The query still needs the right catalog and object access.

Choose columnar files and filter on useful partitions so the query scans less data. Verify which files and columns the query needed. Use a warehouse load instead if the workload needs a managed local table with different performance characteristics.

Different queries compete for shared resources. Use workload management to classify and prioritize workloads. If a report must stay responsive, inspect whether it's waiting in a queue or running slowly; those call for different fixes.

Change the policy only after measuring where time goes. Compare queue wait, execution time and the affected workload under the same load. A change that improves one queue can still leave another starved.

Concurrency scaling can route supported queries to extra capacity during bursts rather than making all eligible work wait. It doesn't mean every query or workload can use the extra cluster. Check workload and query eligibility.

Look at wait time and concurrency scaling usage before changing the cluster. Scaling can relieve contention for eligible traffic, but won't make one inefficient query cheaper or fix its data layout. Verify the queue improvement against the cost.
